newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand's young corporate bond market set to grow.
newsitem.headline: Thailand's young corporate bond market set to grow.

text.p: Thailand's fledgling corporate bond market should expand further next year as demand grows from new pension and fixed-income funds, financial analysts said on Wednesday.
"The corporate bond market will certainly grow more next year," Tawit Thanachanan, head of investment banking at Thai Farmers Bank Plc told Reuters.
"There will be several new pension funds and fixed-income funds launched next year. They will certainly raise demand for new bond issues in the local market," he said.

According to Securities and Exchange Commission data, the total of domestic, baht-denominated bonds issued by Thai companies in the first nine months was 30.4 billion baht ($1.22 billion) compared with 25.05 billion in the same period in 1995.
Tawit said pension and fixed-income funds were currently major players in the bond markets, actively subscribing to new issues and dealing in the secondary bond market as well.
The cabinet on Tuesday approved a proposal requiring eligible companies to set up provident funds for employees.
The Finance Ministry is also speeding up the establishment of pension funds in most state enterprises and large corporations in an attempt to raise long-term savings.
All state enterprises are required to set up pension fund schemes by the end of 1997, and analysts said this would see the establishment and involvement of more funds in the bond market.

The number of fixed-income funds has grown substantially this year as a prolonged slump in the local stock market has prompted retail investors to put their money into lower-risk investments, analysts said.
A fixed-income fund is a mutual fund that invests mainly in fixed-yield financial instruments such as short-term notes and bonds.

Thai Farmers Asset Management Co Ltd data showed that the outstanding amount in fixed-income funds at the end of September jumped to 92.10 billion baht compared with 21.23 billion baht at the end of last year.
Analysts see more room for the growth of fixed-income funds next year on the back of a bearish stock market.

"There will be more funds pouring into the fixed-income funds because of the sluggish stock market, which has small chances of a major recovery in the near term," said Vichate Tantiwanich, first senior vice president at Thai Farmers Asset Management.

Most local issuers of bonds have also been forced to look at the domestic market to raise funds as political and economic uncertainty has significantly affected foreign interest in Thai bonds, analysts said.
